result.summary: Apollo mocks Cupid's bow, and Cupid avenges himself by shooting Apollo with a golden love arrow and Daphne with a leaden arrow that repels love. Apollo chases Daphne, who prays to her father Peneus and is changed into a laurel. Apollo adopts the laurel as his sacred tree.

scenes.title: Apollo Mocks Cupid
scenes.summary: Apollo, proud of killing the Python, scorns Cupid's bow. Cupid flies to Parnassus and shoots Apollo with a gold arrow and Daphne with a lead one.
scenes.stakes: Apollo's pride is at risk; he is about to be struck by love against his will.

scenes.title: Daphne Refuses Marriage
scenes.summary: Daphne loves the woods and hunting and rejects all suitors. She begs her father for lifelong virginity, but her beauty inflames Apollo.
scenes.stakes: Daphne's chosen life of freedom and virginity is threatened by her beauty.

scenes.title: The Chase
scenes.summary: Apollo pleads and boasts of his powers as he chases the fleeing Daphne, like a greyhound after a hare.
scenes.stakes: Daphne risks capture and violation; Apollo risks a fruitless passion.

scenes.title: Daphne Becomes a Laurel
scenes.summary: Exhausted, Daphne prays to her father and the Earth and turns into a laurel. Apollo makes it his tree and promises it evergreen honor.
scenes.stakes: Daphne loses her human form to escape Apollo.

characters.name: Apollo
characters.description: Archer god of prophecy, music and healing, who slew the Python

characters.name: Daphne
characters.description: Huntress nymph, daughter of Peneus, who shuns love

characters.name: Cupid
characters.description: Winged god of love who takes revenge on Apollo

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of the huntress goddess, here Diana, sister of Phœbus.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo's ironic plea: Daphne flees because she does not know who he is.
The god of healing cannot cure his own love.
Apollo links the laurel to Augustus and Roman honors.

analysis.text: Love as power and compulsion: even a proud god is overcome by it, and Daphne's refusal costs her human form.
Apollo's promise ties the laurel to Roman triumphs and to Augustus's doorposts, flattering the emperor.

legacy.text: The laurel wreath became a symbol of victory and poetic honor, giving us 'poet laureate' and 'resting on one's laurels'.
Bernini's marble sculpture Apollo and Daphne (1622-25) depicts the moment of transformation.

fun_facts.text: The Greek word for laurel is daphne, so the myth explains the tree's name.

language_notes.text: "Delian God" means Apollo, who was born on the island of Delos. "Wanton" here means playful and mischievous, not lewd.
The Python was the huge serpent of Mount Parnassus that Apollo killed near Delphi. This victory is the source of his pride.
"I know not what flames" is Apollo's contemptuous way of belittling Cupid's power over love.
"Lead beneath the reed" means the arrow has a lead tip under its reed shaft, making it blunt.
Phœbe is Diana, goddess of hunting and virginity. Daphne imitates her way of life.
Hymen is the god of marriage, whose name stands for the wedding itself.
The "nuptial torch" was carried in Roman wedding processions. Daphne asks for the same lifelong virginity that Jove granted Diana.
Apollo's "oracles" refer to his gift of prophecy. He cannot foresee his own failure.
Delphi, Claros, Tenedos and Patara were famous centres of Apollo's worship and oracles; he claims them as his domain.
Apollo claims knowledge of past, present and future (prophecy) and patronage of music; Jupiter is his father.
Simples are medicinal herbs, each used alone as a remedy; Apollo was also god of healing.
Stock means the trunk of the tree.
The laurel and oak at Augustus's doors refer to honors voted him in 27 BC: laurels flanked his house, and an oak wreath marked saving citizens.
Pæan is a title of Apollo, originally as healer, here used for him as god.

context_notes.text: Peneus is a river god of Thessaly. Daphne is his daughter, a nymph, and her name is Greek for laurel.
Parnassus is the mountain sacred to Apollo and the Muses, near Delphi.
Peneus is a river god in Thessaly, Daphne's father.
The laurel became Apollo's sacred tree, worn in his hair and carried on his lyre and quiver.
Roman generals in a triumph wore laurel crowns and processed to the Capitol, the hill with Jupiter's temple.

literary_notes.text: Cupid's boast that his bow will strike Apollo anticipates the god's own humiliation. Apollo's scorn is about to be turned against him.
The gold and lead arrows give opposite effects, desire and aversion, so the same attack makes one lover and the other fugitive.
Apollo's passion is compared to burning stubble and hedges. The images show a small spark growing into a destructive fire.
Apollo imagines unseen beauty as still lovelier. His desire grows from sight and imagination, which foreshadows the pursuit.
Repeated 'thus' and the string of predator-prey pairs build Apollo's argument, ironically casting himself as the predator he denies being.
The master archer is wounded by Cupid's arrow, a more unerring shot, which reverses his proud claims.
The greyhound and hare compare the chase to a hunt, making Apollo the hunter and Daphne the prey despite his pleading.
Love gives Apollo wings, suggesting desire is a force that propels him faster than Daphne's fear.
Her body changes part by part, with only her elegance left, which makes the change vivid and poignant.
The laurel nods as if a head, suggesting consent and leaving a trace of Daphne's humanity.
